module_title: Foundation Model Customization, Evaluation and Bedrock Applications
part_title: Training Datasets, Transfer Learning and Customization Choices
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 04 through 08 individually in slide order; matched every instructional diagram, numbered panel, example, AWS label and decision cue to the narration.

scenes.title: Single-turn Instruction-tuning Datasets
scenes.narration: This slide shows how to prepare single-turn instruction-tuning data. Single-turn means one user instruction paired with one desired assistant response, rather than a back-and-forth chat. Follow the four numbered boxes from left to right. In box one, we curate example pairs. The invoice says 'Classify: invoice total is incorrect,' and the desired answer is Billing. A package that has not arrived maps to Shipping, while an app that will not open maps to Technical Support. These are training examples with correct labels, not live customer interactions. Next, box two says format for your model. Notice the three message cards: an optional system instruction tells the model to classify customer support tickets, the user message contains the invoice complaint, and the assistant message provides Billing. The exact schema depends on the foundation model you select, so do not assume every model accepts the same training file. Box three stores many correctly formatted examples together in an Amazon S3 bucket. Amazon S3 is cloud object storage; it holds the training file that Bedrock will read. The fourth box uses that file to fine-tune a supported model in Amazon Bedrock. At the bottom, the green panel explains what makes good training data: clear intent, consistent categories and common variations. The red panel distinguishes training from inference. These stored pairs teach the model, but they are not responses to live users. After training, we separately test the model on examples it did not see. Quick check: why must 'Billing' appear in a training pair? Because it is the desired response the model is learning to produce.

scenes.title: Multi-turn Instruction-Tuning Datasets
scenes.narration: Compare this slide to the previous one. A multi-turn example contains several user and assistant messages in order, so the model can learn to follow a conversation rather than treat every message as an isolated request. Start with the left-hand conversation. The user first says 'Help categorize support tickets.' The assistant responds, 'Sure! Share the issue and I'll choose a category.' Next the user says 'My invoice is wrong,' and the assistant replies Billing. The same user then says 'Also, I can't sign in to my account,' and the assistant answers Account Access. The word 'also' matters because the user is continuing an existing conversation. Now follow the arrows across the image. Panel two stores many complete example conversations in Amazon S3. Panel three uses that dataset in a supported customization job, provided the selected model accepts multi-turn training. Panel four shows the customized model, with callouts for understanding previous turns, keeping context and giving consistent answers. Look along the bottom to see the difference. The left panel's single-turn example is one user message leading to one assistant answer. The middle panel preserves multiple alternating turns as one training example. This is useful for a help desk that receives follow-up questions without repeating the full problem each time. But it is not enough to claim the model will always remember every conversation: the application must still supply relevant conversational history at inference time. Ask yourself whether removing the earlier turns would teach the model to handle follow-ups reliably. No. Those turns are precisely the context we want it to learn from.

scenes.title: Fine-Tuning: the Complete Work Involved
scenes.narration: The central message here is that fine-tuning is a full lifecycle, not just pressing a training button. Read the five stages from left to right. Stage one is data preparation. The illustrated customer tickets include Billing question, Technical issue and General enquiry. We must collect representative examples, remove sensitive personal data, label them correctly and avoid letting one category dominate. Stage two is customization compute. The chip and server graphics stand for training resources: choose a supported foundation model, AWS Region and job settings, then run the customization. Stage three is held-out evaluation, shown by the checklist for quality, task fit and errors to inspect. Test on fresh examples, including difficult cases and errors across categories, before deciding the model is good enough. Stage four is deployment. The cloud graphic reminds us that supported serving options vary by model and Region; a completed training job does not automatically give us a production-ready endpoint. Stage five is monitoring. The chart and warning icon indicate tracking accuracy, latency, cost and changes in incoming data, known as drift. Drift can arise when new kinds of tickets appear and the old training examples no longer represent them well. Now look at the comparison along the bottom left. Instruction tuning for a narrow task often needs less data and compute than broader continued training, although the actual cost is workload-specific. The example at the bottom right classifies 'My payment failed, can you help?' as Billing. It illustrates why correct labels and realistic testing matter. A practical question: if you only budget for the training job, have you covered the real cost? No. Data work, evaluation, hosting and ongoing monitoring all matter.

scenes.title: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning
scenes.narration: This picture explains transfer learning with images of flowers, buildings, animals and vehicles. On the left, a pretrained image model has already learned general-purpose visual features such as edges, textures and objects. Training that from scratch needs substantial labeled data and computing power. Follow the large arrow into the middle panel. We now have a smaller, related dataset showing manufactured parts labeled Good or Defect. Instead of discarding the pretrained model, we reuse its existing visual understanding to solve the new defect-detection task. The model layers in blue represent knowledge we are carrying forward, and the purple layer represents the task-specific classifier. On the right are two choices. Choice A is feature extraction. The lock icon indicates the pretrained layers remain frozen, meaning their existing weights do not change, while a new classification layer learns to distinguish good parts from defective ones. Choice B is fine-tuning. The golden layers indicate some or all of the pretrained weights are updated using the new examples, allowing deeper adaptation to the task. Below, the gray blocks labeled random weights show training from scratch, while the colored pretrained blocks show the starting point for transfer learning. Transfer learning is the broad idea of reusing a model's learned representations; fine-tuning is one method within it. If you have few labeled defect images and need a simpler approach, begin with frozen feature extraction. If performance is insufficient and you have adequate data and compute, evaluate fine-tuning. The key is to compare results on held-out images rather than assuming a larger training job must be better.

scenes.title: When Fine-Tuning Helps
scenes.narration: This slide gives three concrete situations where fine-tuning can help. Start with panel one, consistent persona and tone. The robot on the left gives a generic 'Sure! Here are some options' reply, while the fine-tuned robot on the right uses a more consistent support-team style with recommended next steps. This is about the manner of replying, not about learning new facts. In the middle panel, task-specific classification, three different customer messages flow into the model. A damaged item refund request maps to Returns and Refunds, an app connection issue to Technical Support, and an invoice question to Billing and Payments. This is the same category-learning idea from earlier slides, now shown as an application. Panel three compares a general policy explanation with a standardized Policy Summary that consistently includes Policy, Eligibility and Next Steps. Notice that a consistent format is different from guaranteed factual accuracy. The bottom-left diagram explains the mechanism: labeled examples describing desired style, terminology and format are used to update a pretrained model's weights. In the middle-bottom quality panel, three icons emphasize relevant examples, variety including edge cases, and realistic evaluation. Poor labels or biased data can produce unwanted responses despite good-looking output. Finally read the decision panel on the bottom right. Use retrieval when facts change frequently, such as product details, current policies or inventory. Use fine-tuning for stable behaviors, classifications, tone and terminology. As a quick decision: if a policy changes tomorrow, should we expect the fine-tuned model to know it automatically? No. Provide the current policy through retrieval, and keep the customized behavior separate.
